1.title: Building a search engine in Ruby
1.body: Building a small search engine in Ruby is a good way to learn how Elasticsearch works inside. You can learn tokenizing, indexing and scoring by writing the code yourself.

2.title: Inverted index
2.body: An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents that contain it. It is the core data structure of Lucene and Elasticsearch.

3.title: Tokenizer
3.body: A tokenizer splits text into terms. For English text, splitting on spaces and punctuation is enough to start with.

4.title: Scoring with TF-IDF
4.body: TF-IDF gives a higher score to terms that appear often in one document but rarely in the whole collection. This is the first step toward ranking.

5.title: BM25
5.body: BM25 improves TF-IDF by limiting the effect of repeated terms and by adjusting for document length. Elasticsearch uses BM25 as its default similarity.

6.title: Japanese text
6.body: Japanese text has no spaces between words, so a simple tokenizer does not work. A bigram tokenizer splits text into pairs of characters, and a morphological analyzer such as MeCab splits it into real words.

7.title: Ruby gems for search
7.body: Ruby has many client gems for search servers, such as elasticsearch-ruby, opensearch-ruby, searchkick and chewy. There are very few search engines written in pure Ruby.

8.title: Searchkick
8.body: Searchkick is a high level gem for Rails that hides many details of Elasticsearch. Reading its source code shows what the wrapper does for you.

9.title: Full text search in databases
9.body: PostgreSQL has full text search through pg_search, and SQLite has FTS5. PGroonga is strong at Japanese search and is popular in the Japanese Ruby community.

10.title: Library or server
10.body: A search engine can run as a library inside the application, like SQLite or Tantivy, or as a separate server over HTTP, like Elasticsearch. A library is enough when you start learning.

11.title: Full scan first
11.body: Before building an inverted index, start with a full scan that reads every document for each query. It is simple, but it becomes slow when the number of documents grows.

12.title: Measuring performance
12.body: Measure the search time with the Benchmark module while the number of documents grows from one thousand to one hundred thousand. Seeing the slowdown explains why an index is needed.

13.title: Test data from Wikipedia
13.body: Simple English Wikipedia is good test data. The articles are short and easy to read, and there is an official API and an official dump.

14.title: Spinel
14.body: Spinel is a project that compiles Ruby code into native code. A search engine is CPU bound, so it is an interesting target for a benchmark.

15.title: Writing about the project
15.body: Writing down what problem each step solves and why the change works is a good habit. These notes can become a series of articles on Zenn or Qiita.

16.title: Making a gem
16.body: When the code works, move it into a gem with bundle gem. A small API like add and search is easy to use and easy to explain in a talk.
